title: The Room With Too Many Doors

post.author: u/guard_rounds_ines
post.title: I guard a museum of old doors at night. Every night the kiosk says Room 3 has nine more.

blocks.text: I am the night guard at the Calloway Door Museum. It is exactly what it sounds like: front doors, cellar doors and chapel doors saved from houses that were knocked down, standing upright in rooms where they lead nowhere. Room 3 holds nine of them. I count them on every round. It is in my contract.

Last month our volunteer, Theo, built what he calls the collection API. He says it is a front desk for programs instead of people. The touchscreen kiosks and the website don't open the curator's files. They send it requests, and it answers in JSON, plain text made of labels and values. Each door has its own address there, built from its catalog number, like /v1/doors/cdm-004.
On Monday Theo added a job that runs at 3:00 AM. It reads the curator's spreadsheet, nine rows, one per door, and sends every row to the API, so new arrivals appear without anyone typing.
Tuesday night, the kiosk in Room 3 said *18 doors in this room.* I counted nine. Wednesday it said 27. The website now lists the Ashby front door three times, each with a different address.
Tonight I sat in front of the kiosk with Theo's laptop open on the API's log and waited for 3:00.

03:00:01  POST /v1/doors  {"name":"Ashby front door"}    201 Created  /v1/doors/d-19
03:00:01  POST /v1/doors  {"name":"Mercer cellar door"}  201 Created  /v1/doors/d-20
03:00:04  POST /v1/doors  {"name":"Wren back door"}      201 Created  /v1/doors/d-27
Nine requests. Nine times *Created*. The kiosk blinked and redrew the floor plan of Room 3. It shows 36 doors now, packed along four walls, some of them drawn where I know there is only plaster.
Nothing came in through the loading bay. The doors just kept being filed.

Margit, our curator, wants to delete the extras by hand before Friday's school visit. Theo says the job only "saves the spreadsheet to the API", and saving the same nine doors cannot make more doors. It clearly can. What do we change before 3:00 AM tomorrow? And why does saving the same thing make new things?

blocks.label: import_job.png

diagram.aria: The nightly import. The curator's spreadsheet has 9 rows. At 3 AM the import job reads it and sends 9 POST requests to the collection API, which adds 9 new doors to the door list every night. The door list now holds 36 doors, of which 9 are real. The Room 3 kiosk asks the API for the doors in room 3 and draws 36. Room 3 itself still has the 9 doors the guard counted.

blocks.caption: I drew this on the back of a visitor map. The spreadsheet has nine rows. Every night the job sends all nine with POST, and the API files each one as a new door with a new address. Three nights, 27 extra doors. The kiosk believes the list. I believe my flashlight.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Read the first word of each log line, then the word after the number. You told a clerk "file this" nine times a night. He is a very good clerk.

replies.author: u/guard_rounds_ines
replies.text: Theo says POST just means "send". Does it not?

replies.author: u/grey_pager
replies.text: It means "here's something new for this collection, you decide where it goes." Ask what the collection decided. Three times.

comments.author: u/docent_dee
comments.text: I volunteer there on weekends, and Theo's wiki has a cheat sheet. Each request starts with a method, a verb saying what to do. GET reads. POST adds a new item to a collection, and the API picks its address. PUT stores this exact item at this exact address, replacing whatever was there. PATCH changes a few fields. DELETE removes. POST, PUT and PATCH carry the door as JSON in the request's body. A method plus a path, like GET /v1/doors, is called an endpoint. A path like /v1/doors/cdm-004 points at one door. Anything after a ? is a query parameter, a filter, like ?room=3.

comments.author: u/archive_moth
comments.text: For what it's worth, 201 isn't an error. It's the status code an API uses to say "I made something new." Yours is very proud of itself.

comments.author: u/hollow_key
comments.text: Ask Theo what the v1 in every address is for.

replies.author: u/guard_rounds_ines
replies.text: He says it's the version. If he ever changes how the answers look, he'll make /v2/ and leave /v1/ alone, so the kiosks don't break.

reply.prompt: The job runs again at 3:00 AM tomorrow. What should Theo change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Make the job use PUT to each door's own address (/v1/doors/cdm-001 and so on), so sending the same row twice just replaces it. Then delete the 27 copies once, and have the API refuse a POST for a catalog number it already has.
options.part2: Theo changed one word and one path on Thursday afternoon. Margit deleted the 27 copies, and the API now answers a POST for a door it already has with *409 Conflict*. At 3:00 AM I watched nine PUTs go by, nine times *200 OK*, and the kiosk stayed at nine. It has said nine every night since. On my way out I passed the loading bay, where a tenth door leans against the wall, still wrapped. It isn't in the spreadsheet yet. As far as the API knows, it does not exist.
options.senior: PUT to an address the client chooses is idempotent: one request or ten leave the same result. A stable ID that already exists in the real world, the catalog number, is what makes that possible. Clean up once, then make duplicates impossible instead of cleaning up forever.

options.text: Make the job delete every door first, then POST all nine again, so each night starts clean.
options.part2: No more extras. But every night the doors got new addresses, so last week's links on the website all said *404 Not Found*. And on Saturday the Wi-Fi dropped at 3:00:02, after the deletes and before the posts. For six hours the kiosk said *0 doors in this room*. I stood in Room 3 with my flashlight, among nine doors the building insisted weren't there.
options.senior: Delete-and-recreate avoids duplicates, but every door gets a new ID each night, which breaks links and anything else that points at a door, and a failure halfway leaves the collection empty. Replacing in place with PUT has neither problem.

options.text: Change the kiosk to hide doors that share a name. Visitors only ever see the kiosk.
options.part2: The kiosk said nine again. The website still listed every copy, because Theo forgot it asks the API too. By the end of the next month the list held over 300 doors and the kiosk took eight seconds to load. Then Margit bought a second door from the Ashby house, also called the Ashby front door. The kiosk hid it.
options.senior: Hiding duplicates in one screen leaves the data wrong for every other program, lets it keep growing, and hides genuine items that happen to share a name. Fix the writes, not the reads.

options.text: Switch the job off. Margit adds each new door by hand through the API when it arrives.
options.part2: No more nightly copies. Then Margit pressed *Save* on a new door during a Wi-Fi hiccup, watched a wheel spin, and pressed it again. Two copies of the new door. She doesn't trust the button now and checks the website after every save. New arrivals take a week to appear, because she is busy.
options.senior: Doing it by hand stops the nightly copies but not the cause: a retried POST still creates a second door, and people retry when things are slow. The write itself has to be safe to repeat.

sim.title: Send requests to the museum's API
sim.lede: You're Theo at his laptop, sending requests to the API by hand on Monday night, before the job's first run: nine doors, each at its own address. Pick a method and an endpoint, edit the JSON body if the method needs one, and press Send. The API's answer appears under the diagram, and the door list changes when the collection does.
sim.tryThis: POST the Ashby door to /v1/doors twice and watch two new addresses appear. Then PUT the same body to /v1/doors/cdm-001 twice: nothing new. Run the 3 AM job three times to replay the story, switch it to PUT and run it again. Finally PATCH a door into room 5 and GET /v1/doors?room=3.

explain.oneLine: The building never grew. The nightly job asked the API to create nine new doors every night with POST, and the API did exactly that, each time with a fresh address.

steps.title: An API is a front desk for programs.
steps.text: API stands for application programming interface: a fixed set of requests one program may send another, and the answers it gets back. The kiosks and the website never touch the museum's storage directly. They ask the collection API over HTTP, and it answers with a status code and a body in JSON, plain text made of labels and values, like {"name": "Ashby front door", "room": 3}. One front desk means every program sees the same doors and follows the same rules.

steps.title: REST: things have addresses, verbs say what to do.
steps.text: REST is the most common style for web APIs. Everything the API manages is a resource with its own address: /v1/doors is the collection of all doors, /v1/doors/cdm-004 is one door. A method plus a path is an endpoint. The part of a path that names one item, like cdm-004, is a path parameter. A filter added after a question mark, like ?room=3, is a query parameter: it narrows what you read without naming a different thing.

steps.title: Each method means one kind of action.
steps.text: GET reads and changes nothing (200 OK). POST sends something new to a collection, and the server decides its address (201 Created). PUT stores a whole item at an address the client chose, creating it or replacing it (201 or 200). PATCH changes some fields of an item (200). DELETE removes it (204 No Content). Asking for an address that holds nothing gets 404 Not Found, and a body the API can't read gets 400 Bad Request.

steps.title: Some methods are safe to repeat. POST isn't.
steps.text: A method is idempotent if sending the same request ten times leaves things exactly as sending it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by the HTTP standard: the second PUT of the Ashby door overwrites the first with the same thing. POST is not: every POST to /v1/doors means "file a new one", so the job's nine identical requests made nine new doors every night. 9, 18, 27, 36.

steps.title: The v1 in the path is a promise.
steps.text: Programs depend on exactly how answers look. If Theo renamed "room" to "gallery", every kiosk would break overnight. So APIs carry a version. Breaking changes go into a new version while the old one keeps working until every program has moved. Some APIs put it in the path (/v1/), GitHub's uses a header, and Microsoft's Azure guidelines use a query parameter with a date.

diagram.aria: Two nights compared. With POST, the job sends POST /v1/doors for the Ashby door and gets 201 Created with a new address, d-19. Sending the same request again gets another 201 Created, d-28: two copies. With PUT, the job sends PUT /v1/doors/cdm-001 and gets 200 OK, replaced. Sending it again gets 200 OK again, still one door. Outcome: POST added a door each time, PUT left one door.

steps.sub: the address comes from the catalog

steps.text: POST: a new door every time

explain.caption: Read top to bottom. The same POST on two nights files two new Ashby doors, d-19 and d-28, because POST means "add one" and the API picks the address. The same PUT on two nights writes to cdm-001 both times, because the address comes from the request. Same request, same result: that is idempotent.

fix.title: The fix: write to addresses you choose, with PUT
fix.text: Give every door a stable ID that already exists outside the API, the catalog number, and make the job send PUT /v1/doors/cdm-001 with the full door in the body. Running the job once or fifty times now leaves the same nine doors. Then clean up once: list the doors with GET, and DELETE the 27 copies. Finally, make duplicates impossible: have the API reject a POST whose catalog number is already taken with 409 Conflict. Microsoft's Azure REST guidelines give the same advice: prefer PUT or PATCH to create things, because they let the client name the resource and are idempotent.

limits: PUT replaces the whole item. Leave a field out of the body and it may be wiped. To change one field, use PATCH, and when two programs edit the same door at once, the last write silently wins (a later season covers how to stop that).

Idempotent means the same end state, not the same answer or no side effects. A second DELETE gets 404 instead of 204, and a client must treat that as fine. A repeated PUT still runs twice, so anything it triggers, like a notification, can happen twice.

Sometimes the client can't choose the address, like a payment that has no natural ID. Then the usual tool is an idempotency key: a unique key sent with the POST that the server remembers, so a retry returns the first result instead of acting again. Season 4 covers it.

head: How the job writes
Good
Bad
rows: Simple. The server picks the IDs.
Every retry or rerun creates a copy. Needs extra protection to be safe to repeat.
Safe to rerun. Addresses stay stable, so links never break.
The client needs a stable ID. PUT replaces the whole item, so the body must be complete.
New IDs every night break links. A failure halfway leaves the collection empty.

explain.seniorTake: Before you write a request, ask what happens if it is sent twice, because sooner or later it will be: a retry after a timeout, a job rerun, a double click. Choose methods and IDs so the second time is harmless.

realWorld.title: GitHub's REST API
realWorld.text: GitHub's REST API follows the same pattern as Theo's. Its getting-started guide lists GET for retrieving resources, POST for creating them, PATCH for updating properties, PUT for replacing, and DELETE for deleting. POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues creates an issue, where the curly brackets mark path parameters you fill in, and query parameters such as per_page control what comes back. Every response carries a status code.

realWorld.title: GitHub's versions are dates
realWorld.text: GitHub versions its REST API by date instead of v1 and v2, and the client picks one with a header, X-GitHub-Api-Version. Requests without the header get the 2022-11-28 version. Its documentation lists what counts as a breaking change that needs a new version, such as removing or renaming a response field, or adding a new required parameter.

realWorld.title: Google's resource-oriented design
realWorld.text: Google's API design guide (now published as AIP-121) says APIs should be built from resources, each either a single resource or a collection of them, and should prefer a small set of standard methods (Get, List, Create, Update, Delete) over custom ones. Its rules for Create (AIP-133) require letting the client choose the resource ID on management APIs, partly so clients can find and update what they made instead of creating it again, and say the service must answer ALREADY_EXISTS when the resource is already there.

realWorld.title: Microsoft's Azure REST guidelines
realWorld.text: Microsoft's Azure REST API guidelines say every HTTP method should be idempotent, that PUT or PATCH is the easier way to create a resource because it lets the customer name it, and that a POST used to create must be made idempotent, for example with repeatability headers. They version APIs with a required api-version query parameter holding a date, like ?api-version=2021-06-04.

realWorld.title: Stripe's idempotency keys
realWorld.text: Stripe, a payments company, can't ask clients to pick IDs for charges, so it accepts an Idempotency-Key header on every POST. It saves the status code and body of the first request with each key, and a retry with the same key gets that same result back instead of acting twice. It notes that GET and DELETE need no key, because they are idempotent by definition.

asked: Design the REST API for a simple collection, like a museum catalog or a to-do list. Which endpoints, and what do they return?
What does idempotent mean? Which HTTP methods are idempotent, and why does it matter?
interview.answer: Start with resources and their addresses: /v1/doors for the collection, /v1/doors/{id} for one item. Map methods to actions: GET list and GET item (200), POST to the collection when the server picks the ID (201 with the new address), PUT to the item when the client knows the ID (create or replace), PATCH for partial updates, DELETE (204). Use query parameters for filters and paging, path parameters to name things, and give the API a version. Then idempotency: a request is idempotent if repeating it leaves the same state as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are; POST isn't. It matters because networks fail and clients retry, so a retried POST creates duplicates unless you use client-chosen IDs or idempotency keys. Mention the limits: PUT replaces the whole item, a second DELETE returns 404, and side effects can still repeat.

terms.def: Application programming interface: a fixed set of requests one program may send another, and the answers it gets back. A front desk for programs instead of people.
The museum's API in this story. The kiosks, the website and the nightly job all read and change the list of doors through it.
A touchscreen in a gallery that shows information to visitors. Here it asks the API which doors are in its room and draws them.
JavaScript Object Notation: plain text made of labels and values, like {"name": "Ashby front door", "room": 3}. Most web APIs send and receive it.
The data sent along with a request, such as the JSON describing a door. GET and DELETE usually have none; POST, PUT and PATCH carry one.
What the API sends back to a request: a status code, headers, and usually a body in JSON.
Representational State Transfer: the most common style for web APIs. Things are resources with their own addresses, and standard HTTP methods say what to do with them.
One thing an API manages, with its own address, like the door at /v1/doors/cdm-004. A collection is a resource that holds others.
A resource that holds a list of similar resources, like /v1/doors. You read it with GET and add to it with POST.
The part of an address after the site's name, like /v1/doors/cdm-004. It says which resource you mean.
One method plus one path that an API accepts, like GET /v1/doors or PUT /v1/doors/{id}. An API is a list of endpoints.
The part of a path that names one item, like cdm-004 in /v1/doors/cdm-004. Documentation often shows it in curly brackets: /v1/doors/{id}.
A filter or option added after a question mark, like /v1/doors?room=3. It changes what you get back without naming a different resource.
The verb at the start of an HTTP request that says what to do: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE and a few others.
The HTTP method for reading. It changes nothing, so it is safe to send as often as you like.
The HTTP method for sending something new to a collection. The server decides what to do with it, usually creating an item with a new address. Not idempotent.
The HTTP method for storing a whole item at an address the client chose, creating it or replacing what was there. Idempotent.
The HTTP method for changing some fields of an existing item, like moving a door to room 5, without sending the whole item.
The HTTP method for removing the item at an address. Idempotent: once it's gone, deleting again changes nothing, though the answer becomes 404.
Safe to repeat: sending the same request ten times leaves things exactly as sending it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not.
A second copy of the same real thing stored under a different ID, like the Ashby front door filed three times.
A short name that identifies one item for good, like cdm-004 or d-19. Its address is built from it.
The museum's own number for each object, like cdm-004. It exists outside the API, so it makes a stable ID.
The status code for a request that worked. For GET it carries what you asked for; for PUT or PATCH, the updated item.
The status code for a request that made something new. It usually comes with the new item's address.
The status code for a request that worked and has nothing to send back, typical after a DELETE.
The status code for a request the server can't understand, such as a body that isn't valid JSON.
The status code for an address with nothing there.
The status code for a method the address doesn't accept, such as PUT on the whole collection.
The status code for a request that clashes with what's already there, such as creating a door whose catalog number is taken.
A label like v1 or a date that fixes how an API's requests and answers look. Breaking changes go into a new version so existing programs keep working.
A change to an API that makes existing programs fail, like renaming a field or adding a required parameter.
A table of rows and columns in a program like Excel. Here, the curator's list of doors, one row per door.
A program that runs on a schedule, here every night at 3:00 AM, and copies data from one place into another.
Sending a request again because the first one seemed to fail, often after a timeout. If the first one actually worked, a retried POST makes a copy.
Giving up on a request after waiting too long for the answer. The request may still have reached the server and worked.
A unique value a client sends with a request so the server can recognise a retry and return the first result instead of acting twice.
Anything a request causes besides its main result, such as sending a notification or writing a log line.
Headers in Microsoft's Azure guidelines (Repeatability-Request-ID and Repeatability-First-Sent) that let a server recognise a repeated POST, like an idempotency key.
A website for storing and working on code with others. Its REST API lets programs manage repositories, issues and more.
On GitHub, a tracked task or bug report attached to a repository.
On GitHub, a project's folder of code and its history.
API Improvement Proposal: one numbered design rule in Google's API design guide, like AIP-121 for resource-oriented design.
A company whose API lets businesses take card payments.
An AWS service that receives HTTP requests for your API, checks them and passes them to the code behind each endpoint.
An AWS database that stores items by key. Its PutItem replaces any item with the same key, so it behaves like PUT; a condition can make it refuse instead.
A standard file format for describing an API's endpoints, parameters and responses, used to generate documentation and client code.

atWork: Open one API your team owns in Amazon API Gateway (or its OpenAPI file) and list its endpoints by method and path. For every POST, write down what happens if the client sends it twice, for example after a timeout: does it create a second record, send a second email, charge twice? Then check how the code behind it saves data. If it uses DynamoDB, PutItem with the item's own key replaces instead of duplicating, and a condition such as attribute_not_exists can turn a repeat into a clean rejection. Finally, find where the API's version lives (path, header or query parameter) and what your clients would see after a breaking change.

recall.prompt: A mobile app's "Place order" button sends POST /v1/orders. On slow networks users tap twice or the app retries after a timeout, and some customers get two identical orders. What is happening, and how would you fix it?

keyIdeas.idea: POST is not idempotent: each one creates a new order
The first request worked even though the client didn't see the answer
Make the create safe to repeat: client-chosen ID with PUT, or an idempotency key
Reject or recognise the repeat on the server

recall.model: Each POST means "create a new order", and POST isn't idempotent. When the network is slow, the first request often reaches the server and succeeds, but the answer is lost or late, so the app or the user sends it again and the server creates a second order. Fix it so the create is safe to repeat: the app generates a unique ID for the order when the button is first pressed and either sends PUT /v1/orders/{that id}, or sends it as an idempotency key with the POST. The server stores the key with the first result and answers any repeat with that same result (or 409 Conflict) instead of creating another order.

recall.prompt: The museum's job sent the same POST /v1/doors for the Ashby door on three nights. What did the API do?
options: Updated the Ashby door three times
Created three new doors, each with its own new address
Ignored the second and third requests
Returned 409 Conflict the second and third times
recall.why: POST to a collection means "add a new one", and the server picks the address. Nothing told the API these were the same door, so it filed a new one each night with 201 Created.

recall.prompt: In GET /v1/doors/cdm-004?fields=name, which part is the path parameter and which is the query parameter?
options: Path parameter: v1. Query parameter: doors
Path parameter: cdm-004. Query parameter: fields=name
Path parameter: fields=name. Query parameter: cdm-004
recall.why: cdm-004 is inside the path and names one resource. fields=name comes after the question mark and only changes what you get back about it.

options: POST /v1/doors with a door in the body
PUT /v1/doors/cdm-001 with a door in the body
Two different PATCH requests that each add one to a counter
Pressing Save twice on a form that POSTs
recall.why: PUT stores the whole door at an address the client chose. Sending it again writes the same thing to the same place, so the end state is the same as sending it once.

recall.prompt: Theo wants to rename the JSON field "room" to "gallery" because the museum renamed its rooms. Six kiosks and the website read "room". How should he roll this out?

keyIdeas.idea: It's a breaking change: existing programs read "room"
Put it in a new version and keep the old one working
Move the clients over, then retire the old version

recall.model: Renaming a field is a breaking change: every kiosk that reads "room" would break the moment it disappears. So he publishes /v2/doors with "gallery" while /v1/doors keeps answering with "room", moves the kiosks and the website to v2 one by one, watches until nothing calls v1 any more, and only then retires it. Adding "gallery" alongside "room" in v1 is a gentler first step, since adding a field doesn't break readers.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The doors stay at nine. Now the gift shop wants its own app to log each ticket sale with POST /v1/sales, and Theo has made the shop's card reader retry automatically whenever the API takes longer than 2 seconds to answer. On Saturday the museum's Wi-Fi was slow all afternoon. On Sunday the sales list showed 212 tickets sold. The till holds money for 140.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What happened, and what should Theo change?

keyIdeas.idea: The slow requests had actually succeeded before the retry
Give each sale a unique ID or idempotency key so repeats are recognised
Clean up the extra sales once

coldCase.model: Slow isn't failed. On Saturday many POSTs took longer than 2 seconds but still reached the API and created the sale, then the card reader retried and created it again: 72 extra sales. Give every sale a unique ID when the card reader starts it (the receipt number works) and either send PUT /v1/sales/{receipt number}, or send it as an idempotency key with the POST so the API returns the first result for a repeat instead of creating another sale. Then clean up the 72 copies once, using the receipt numbers to find them.
